name: Elena Dubois

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I work for the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I buy fresh produce and dry goods for Marché Verdi, a food distributor that supplies restaurants and canteens across three counties. My day starts at 5:30 with the market prices on my phone, because tomatoes can swing 20 percent overnight. By nine I've placed the day's orders with growers and importers, and the rest is chasing late trucks and handling chefs who want a substitute for something that didn't arrive. I've been doing it for 26 years.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What part of that day do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the early mornings and the growers. Marisol, who runs a pepper farm, still sends me a box at Christmas. What wears me out is the pressure to buy cheaper every quarter, and the fact that I haven't had a real raise in four years. My partner Sam works part-time at the library, so we're always doing sums at the kitchen table.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fine, good, it saves me an hour of typing. I already use an AI tool now and then to draft supplier emails and compare quotes. It makes mistakes, so I check everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my worry isn't AI at all. It's that Sam and I have about two weeks of money in the account, my pay is low for what I do, and there are only two other distributors within driving distance. If Marché Verdi has a bad year, I'm stuck.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going and use the AI tool for the boring parts, like the price comparison sheets. I'd try to move 50 a week into a separate account for emergencies. And I'd ask my boss, Renata, for a small raise tied to the savings I find on produce.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy. Nothing is changing, which means nothing is getting better either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned a thank-you card instead of a raise. What did you do with that feeling?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last year I saved the firm about 12,000 on citrus by switching a supplier, and I got a thank-you card instead of a raise. That's the sort of thing that makes me want to look around, if there were anywhere to look.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you hold responsible for the squeeze you describe?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly the firm and the market. Supermarkets squeeze distributors, distributors squeeze buyers, and the person at the bottom of the chain is a woman of 58 with an average pay packet. I'm not blaming a robot.

say: I'd say AI saves me an **hour** of typing, but I check everything it produces.
I'd say the squeeze comes from **supermarkets**, not from software.
think: We have about **two weeks** of money saved, and only two other distributors are in driving distance.
A bad year at my firm would leave me with **nowhere** to go.
do: Use the AI tool for **price comparison** sheets and supplier emails.
Move **50 a week** into a separate emergency account.
Ask my boss for a raise tied to the **savings** I find.
feel: Slightly **uneasy**, because nothing changing also means nothing improving.
S0.quote: Last year I saved the firm about 12,000 on citrus by switching a supplier, and I got a thank-you card instead of a raise.
fieldNote: Her job looks safe in the mild world, but a thin cushion and few local **employers** keep her uneasy.
Already uses AI sometimes and sees it as a tool; blames **supermarket** squeeze, not technology.
The citrus story shows she feels **undervalued** for real savings.

steps.text: Use the AI tool to build weekly price comparison sheets
Move 50 a week into a separate emergency account
Ask Renata for a raise tied to the citrus savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's coming for the middle of the chain, and buyers are in the middle. Choosing, pricing, ordering, chasing: that's what the card describes. I'd tell my colleagues to learn the tools before the tools are learned about us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think about half of what I do can be done by software within three years. The part software can't do is knowing who to call when a frost wipes out a crop. I think the firm will keep two buyers where it has five now. I'd want to be one of the two buyers they keep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up for the evening course the community college runs on supply chain analytics, which costs 400 and which I'd pay out of savings. I'd start using AI daily and show Renata what I do with it. And I'd keep my contacts warm, because relationships are what the software lacks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A mix. A little excited about the tools, a little sick about the headcount.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about a moment when your experience beat the numbers.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last week a younger colleague, Dmitri, asked how I know a supplier is about to fail. I said it's the third late invoice in a row, and the way they stop returning calls. That's the sort of thing the software can't see yet. But I'm not sure that's enough to keep me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said nobody is to blame yet. What would change that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Dmitri to learn the tools faster than me, and to build contacts. As for who's to blame, nobody yet. It's up to the firm what it does with the savings, and I'd say they should keep us, but I'm not naive about it.

say: I'd tell colleagues to **learn the tools** before the tools are learned about us.
I'd say relationships with growers are what software **lacks**.
think: Roughly **half** of my work could be done by software within three years.
I expect the firm to keep two buyers where it has five, and I want to be one.
do: Sign up for a **400** evening course on supply chain analytics, paid from savings.
Use AI daily and show my boss what I do with it.
Keep my **grower contacts** warm by calling them each month.
feel: A **mix**: curious about the tools, sick about the likely headcount cuts.
S1.quote: The part software can't do is knowing who to call when a frost wipes out a crop.
fieldNote: Judges that her **thinking-heavy** job will be cut by more than half, but feels she has some control and acts.
Fair on blame for now: wants to see what the firm does with the **savings**.
Her tacit **knowledge**, such as spotting a failing supplier, is her bet for staying.

steps.text: Enrol in the 400 supply chain analytics evening course
Use the AI tool every day and show Renata the results
Call five key growers every month to keep contacts warm
Put aside 400 from savings for the course fee

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a shock, and be honest that nobody is ready. I'd also say, loudly, that companies need to be told they can't just drop people. Two years is a blink.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my job is gone by the end of 2028, or turned into a tiny checking role for one person. I'd be 60. I'd have maybe three weeks of savings, and Sam's library hours would go too if the council cut back. That's what frightens me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First, I'd go to Renata and ask what the firm's plan is for the buyers. Then I'd write to my union rep, since we're in the general workers' union, and ask for a retraining fund. I'd also look at what hands-on work I could learn, like warehouse supervision, because those jobs last about three more years. And I'd sell the little holiday cottage share my brother and I own, if it came to it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, jittery, hard to sleep. I'm the sort who plans, and this resists planning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd sell your share in the cottage. What else would you do for money in the first year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my daughter Claire not to count on me for any help, and I'd tell her to keep her own job. She's in a hospital lab, which feels safer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want the government to do, and do you believe it will?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd blame the way the rules are set up. Companies get all the savings from AI and the public gets the bill, and I don't trust governments to act in time. I'd want governments to tax some of that and pay people who lose their jobs.

say: I'd say nobody is **ready**, and companies must be told they can't simply drop people.
I'd say **two years** is a blink.
think: My job is gone or shrunk to one **checking** role by the end of 2028.
If the council cut library hours, **Sam's pay** would shrink too, and that frightens me.
do: Ask Renata what the firm's plan is for the **buyers**.
Ask my union rep to push for a **retraining fund**.
Look at warehouse supervision, which lasts about **3 years** longer than desk work.
feel: **Anxious** and sleepless, because a planner like me finds this hard to plan for.
S2.quote: Companies get all the savings from AI and the public gets the bill, and I don't trust governments to act in time.
fieldNote: **Expects** her job to vanish and Sam's hours to be at risk too, so alarmed.
Looks toward hands-on work for the **three-year** robot delay.
Wants **redistribution** but doesn't trust governments to act in time.

steps.text: Ask Renata in writing what happens to the buyers
Ask the union rep to demand a company-funded retraining pool
Shadow the warehouse supervisor one afternoon a week
Sell my half of the family cottage

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years I can work with. I'd say it's like a coming storm: you see it, so you board the windows. I'd tell friends to start preparing now rather than complain later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be 63 when it arrives. I think I could stretch to a smaller pension and keep a few part-time hours if I plan well. It's still scary because the numbers on my savings are tiny, but at least it isn't tomorrow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the time well. Evening course in the first year, then a certificate in food safety and supplier audits, which is the human side of buying. I'd save 150 a month, and I'd begin selling my homemade chutneys at the Saturday market, since I already make dozens of jars. It's not much, but it's mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steadier than two years. Anxious, but with a handle to hold.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me more about the market stall. What does it actually bring in?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The market stall brought in 90 last Saturday. That's not a living, but it's proof I can do something outside the firm. Sam says I should call it a business and put a price on the labels.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make the firm keep a role like supplier audits?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it goes the way I fear, I'd tell Renata I want to move into supplier audits, where a person has to be present. I think the firm would keep that role longer, and I'd fight for it. Otherwise I'd leave with a little saved and a market stall.

say: I'd tell friends AI is like a coming storm: you can see it, so **board the windows**.
I'd say start preparing now instead of complaining later.
think: I'd be **63** on arrival, so a small pension plus part-time hours might work.
Savings are tiny, but five years means it isn't **tomorrow**.
do: Take the evening course and then a **food safety** and supplier audit certificate.
Save **150 a month** from now on.
Sell homemade **chutneys** at the Saturday market.
feel: **Steadier** than in the two-year world: anxious, but with a handle to hold.
S3.quote: The market stall brought in 90 last Saturday. That's not a living, but it's proof I can do something outside the firm.
fieldNote: Five years lets her turn a hobby into proof of a second income, which **steadies** her.
Aims at supplier audits, a **human-presence** role, as a place to land.
Still has a thin **cushion**, so mood stays anxious not calm.

steps.text: Finish the evening course and get a supplier audit certificate
Save 150 a month in a separate account
Sell chutneys at the Saturday market every week
Ask Renata to move me into supplier audits

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years: I'd say it's a long runway. I'd tell people not to panic, but not to coast either. It's enough time to reinvent yourself if you start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be 68 and likely retired, so my own job isn't the issue. What bothers me is the world my partner Sam and I retire into, with thin savings and prices that might jump. I'd feel safe about work but not about money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work until 66, using AI as my assistant. I'd keep the chutney stall as a little income, and I'd put 200 a month into a pension top-up. I'd also help Claire buy a flat, if I could, which means saving harder. And I'd join the union's campaign for a decent state pension.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm about the job. A bit uneasy about being old and poor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said calm about work, uneasy about money. Which weighs heavier?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sam and I talked about it last weekend. We'd like to move to a smaller place near Claire when I stop working. That depends on the housing market, which I can't control.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with a retraining fund, if one existed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say nobody should be left to figure this out alone for ten years. If the government sets a retraining fund now, I'd use it. If it doesn't, I'd blame them first and the firm second.

say: I'd tell people not to panic and not to coast: ten years is a **long runway**.
I'd back the union's campaign for a decent **state pension**.
think: At 68 my own job isn't the issue; our **retirement money** is.
I'd feel safe about work but nervous about prices and **thin savings**.
do: Work until **66**, using AI as my assistant.
Put **200 a month** into a pension top-up.
Keep the chutney stall as **extra income**.
feel: Mostly **calm** about the job, a little uneasy about being old and short of money.
S4.quote: What bothers me is the world my partner Sam and I retire into, with thin savings and prices that might jump.
fieldNote: **Retirement** falls inside the window so her job is less at risk, but money in old age worries her.
Plans around family: a smaller home near her **daughter** Claire.
Would use a **retraining** fund, and blames government first if none exists.

steps.text: Work until 66 and use AI to keep up with the job
Pay 200 a month into a pension top-up
Keep running the chutney stall at the Saturday market
Join the union's campaign for a better state pension

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because there's no time for someone who has almost nothing saved. What would help is a real retraining fund, paid for by the companies that save money, and a pension that doesn't punish people for losing work at 58. I'd also want a person at the firm to tell us honestly who stays.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that people like me aren't scared of the tools. I use them. I'm scared of being the cheapest thing on the balance sheet when the savings show up.

headlineQuote: I'm scared of being the cheapest thing on the balance sheet when the savings show up.
portrait: **Elena Dubois**, 58, buys produce and dry goods for a food distributor, with 26 years in the trade.
She is **progressive** and steady: she already uses AI tools sometimes and moves when change is proven.
Her thin cushion, low pay and few local employers keep her **anxious** even when the work looks safe.
She plans practically: evening courses, a chutney stall, audit roles, and union and pension campaigns.
She blames **supermarkets**, companies and slow governments, not the technology itself.
biggestWorry: The **2028** world, because two years leaves no time for someone with almost nothing saved.
whatWouldHelp: A **retraining fund** paid by firms that save money, and a pension that doesn't punish job loss at 58.
An honest conversation at work about **who stays**.
